demonstrations._program_note: Longitudinal cohort study (UK, n=236) using PIRLS student questionnaire items as instruments; PIRLS 2006 data used as measurement baseline. Reading motivation and reading experience from PIRLS questionnaire; ToM measured via Silent Films task at age 13.

evidence_pairs._ilsa_variable_note: PIRLS reading motivation items used as instrument; explicit PIRLS variable codes not stated in source.
evidence_pairs.evidence_text: There was a significant unique concurrent association between fiction reading and ToM even when individual differences in verbal ability and reading motivation were considered (Table 3).

We also tested whether the link between reading fiction and ToM was unique by controlling for verbal ability, reading comprehension, reading motivation, verbal ability, child age (at Time 3), gender (i.e., 0 = girl, 1 = boy), and parental education (i.e., low, medium, or high).

evidence_pairs._ilsa_variable_note: PIRLS reading motivation items used as instrument; explicit PIRLS variable codes not stated in source.
evidence_pairs.effect_size: b = .10 (SE = .09), 95% CI [−.10, .26] (Table 4, longitudinal model, Time 1 → Time 3; not significant)
evidence_pairs.evidence_text: Self-reported fiction reading and nonfiction reading at Time 1 did not uniquely predict ToM at Time 3 (Table 4). Instead, individual differences in ToM were uniquely associated with receptive vocabulary, parental education, and gender.

evidence_pairs.effect_size: b = −.17 (SE = .07), 95% CI [−.28, −.05] (Table 4, longitudinal model, Time 1 → Time 3)
evidence_pairs.evidence_text: individual differences in ToM were uniquely associated with receptive vocabulary, parental education, and gender.

evidence_pairs.effect_size: b = .17 (SE = .08), 95% CI [.04, .29] (Table 4, longitudinal model, Time 1 → Time 3)
evidence_pairs.evidence_text: individual differences in ToM were uniquely associated with receptive vocabulary, parental education, and gender.

Children who reported reading more fiction in their own time performed better on the ToM task over and above other confounding variables such as verbal ability, reading comprehension, and parent education.
